content: Labial fusion is a medical condition affecting the female genital anatomy, characterized by the fusion of the labia minora. This condition is primarily observed in pediatric patients. It is referred to by various terms, including labial fusion, labial adhesion, labial synechiae, labial agglutination, labial adherence, gynatresia, vulvar fusion, and vulvar synechiae. Labial fusion is not present at birth but develops later during infancy. This is due to insufficient estrogen exposure, as newborns are exposed to maternal estrogen in utero. The condition typically manifests in infants who are at least three months old. Most cases are asymptomatic and are discovered either by a parent or during routine medical examinations. However, some patients may present with symptoms such as dysuria (painful urination), increased urinary frequency, refusal to urinate, or post-void dribbling. In certain cases, vaginal discharge may occur due to the pooling of urine in the vulvar vestibule or vagina. The diagnosis of labial fusion is made through visual inspection of the vulva. When the labia majora are retracted, a flat plane of tissue with a dense central line is usually observed. An anterior opening is often visible below the clitoris. The primary underlying cause of labial fusion is low estrogen levels. In preadolescent individuals, the vulva has a delicate epithelial lining due to minimal estrogen exposure, making it susceptible to irritation. Factors such as infection, inflammation, or trauma can lead to irritation, causing the edges of the labia minora to adhere and fuse. The fusion typically begins at the posterior frenulum of the labia minora and progresses anteriorly. Most labial adhesions resolve spontaneously before puberty as estrogen levels rise and the vaginal epithelium becomes keratinized. Treatment is generally unnecessary in asymptomatic cases, as most fusions separate naturally over time. However, treatment may be required if symptoms are present. The standard treatment involves the application of topical estrogen cream to the areas of adhesion, which is effective in approximately 90% of cases. In severe cases, where the labia minora are completely fused, leading to urinary outflow obstruction or vaginal obstruction, surgical separation of the labia may be necessary. Recurrence after treatment is common but can be minimized with good hygiene practices. Some studies suggest that betamethasone may be more effective than estrogen cream in preventing recurrence, with fewer side effects. Complications of labial fusion include urinary tract infections, vulvar vestibulitis, and inflammation caused by chronic urine exposure. In severe cases, labial adhesions can result in complete obstruction of the urethra, leading to anuria (inability to urinate) and urinary retention. Labial fusion is not uncommon in infants and young girls, with a prevalence of approximately 3% in this age group and up to 8% in prepubertal girls. It is rare in adult women, particularly those of reproductive age, but may occasionally be observed in postpartum and postmenopausal women.
